title: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Has Tens of Millions Invested in AI Industry
author: Mark Olalde
content:
The Trump administration has likened the need to build out the nation’s
artificial intelligence infrastructure to the Manhattan Project, the World War
II effort that produced the world’s first atomic bomb.

The White House’s point person on the effort, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum,
has spoken of the [“AI arms race”](https://www.c-span.org/program/senate-
committee/interior-secretary-nominee-doug-burgum-testifies-at-confirmation-
hearing/654498) with China as an existential issue for the nation. “AI is
manufacturing intelligence, and, if we don’t manufacture more intelligence
than our adversaries, it affects every job, every company and every industry,”
he said during his Senate [confirmation
hearing](https://www.propublica.org/article/doug-burgum-north-dakota-interior-
department-trump) in January 2025.

But advancing the administration’s AI objectives also could benefit Burgum’s
own finances.

Much of his wealth is held in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-
founded, [according to his 2026 financial disclosure
form](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/burgum-doug/), which has not been previously reported.
Between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those investments are in AI
companies, according to an analysis of the companies’ marketing materials
shared with ProPublica by public lands advocacy group Save Our Parks.
(Government financial disclosure forms allow filers to report wide ranges
instead of the specific value of their investments.)

Burgum made his fortune 25 years ago when he sold a software company to
Microsoft and has remained heavily invested in technology. In the year before
joining the administration, when he was North Dakota’s governor, he made
between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related
investments, Save Our Parks’ analysis showed. In 2025, he sold millions of
dollars of stocks and equity in AI companies, bringing in capital gains worth
between $2.5 million and $15.1 million.

In the ethics agreement Burgum signed as part of his Senate confirmation, he
agreed to resign from his positions at Arthur but not give up his financial
interests there.

“Secretary Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure
obligations,” a U.S. Department of the Interior spokesperson told ProPublica
in a statement. “Any suggestion that his office decisions are driven by
personal investments are false and completely unsupported.”

Officials across the Trump administration also stand to profit from the White
House’s support for AI and data centers. For example, 380 of President Donald
Trump’s political appointees or their spouses hold [stocks or have other
financial connections to Nvidia](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-
financial-disclosures/search/?q=nvidia), which has become the world’s most
valuable company thanks to the data center boom. More than 320 have [ties to
Alphabet](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/search/?q=alphabet), Google’s parent company, which plans to spend
at least $195 billion this year building data centers and AI-related
technology. And more than 240 are [invested in or otherwise have financial
ties to Meta Platforms](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/search/?q=meta%2C+inc), which is developing a “fleet” of data
centers. This is according to an analysis of records added last week to the
[Trump Team Financials database developed by
ProPublica](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-disclosures/)
to make accessible the financial disclosures of administration officials.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/20251002-Hickey-
Disclosures_3-FINAL_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-1.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1)
**Explore Financial Disclosures From President Trump and 2,300 of His
Appointees** ](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/)

Federal officials’ activities are governed by a criminal statute that sets a
high burden of proof for potential wrongdoing — for example, approving permits
for a company in which they are substantially invested, multiple ethics
professors and lawyers told ProPublica. They said that Burgum’s investments
appear to be acceptable under this law.

But ethics rules that do not carry criminal penalties also apply, explained
Cynthia Brown, senior ethics counsel with Citizens for Responsibility and
Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog group. These rules, she said,
“instruct officials not to work on anything that would create the appearance
of a conflict of interest.” She said this would include Burgum’s support for
data centers on federal land while holding investments in AI.

Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and President
George W. Bush’s chief ethics lawyer, agreed that Burgum should avoid making
decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. “I, as the
ethics lawyer, would insist he stay away from it,” Painter said. “In the Bush
administration, the answer would’ve been ‘he has to recuse,’ I can guarantee
you that.”

A review of recent Interior Department secretaries’ financial holdings
suggests it’s common to have some potential conflicts, but Trump’s appointees
are more heavily invested in the industries they oversee than their
predecessors. Deb Haaland, President Joe Biden’s appointee, [held no direct
financial investments](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28862540-deb-
haaland-financial-disclosure/) in companies the department regulated.
President Barack Obama’s first appointee, Ken Salazar, listed [ownership of
his family’s
ranch](https://s3.amazonaws.com/propublica/assets/financial_disclosures/Salazar_Kenneth_INT.pdf)
but few other investments. Obama’s second appointee, Sally Jewell, [held
stocks in oil and
gas](https://www.houstonchronicle.com/business/energy/article/interior-
nominee-owns-oil-and-gas-stocks-4331377.php), which she agreed to divest as a
condition of her confirmation.

Ryan Zinke and David Bernhardt served as Interior Department secretaries
during Trump’s first term. The former [was found by the agency’s Office of
Inspector General](https://www.npr.org/2022/02/16/1081180054/ryan-zinke-
interior-investigation-ig-report) to have improperly assisted a development in
his hometown, while the latter had so many potential conflicts that [he
reportedly carried a card listing
them](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/the-man-behind-
the-curtain-interiors-no-2-helps-drive-trumps-
agenda/2018/11/18/6403eb4c-e9ff-11e8-b8dc-66cca409c180_story.html). (Zinke
said the OIG investigation was a political attack, while Bernhardt recused
himself from several decisions in which there would have been clear
conflicts.)

More recently, as the effort to build data centers has run headlong into broad
public opposition, [the current administration has
offered](https://www.washingtonsun.com/climate-environment/trump-
administration-data-centers-public-lands-proposals) federally managed public
lands to them. Unlike local or state processes, where concerns about water
use, power consumption and the lack of transparency around permitting have
slowed or halted projects, the public has less ability to stop them on federal
property. The Interior Department [oversees most of this
land](https://www.washingtonsun.com/technology/data-centers-public-lands-
trump).

![A bearded man yells while surrounded by a crowd of protesters holding signs
opposed to data center construction in their
community.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2274045659.jpg?w=1149)Members of the
public protest a secretive deal to permit a massive data center in northern
Utah, including voicing concerns that it would require large volumes of water
in the parched region. Natalie Behring/Getty Images

A little-noticed U.S. Geological Survey [report released earlier this
year](https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2026/5035/sir20265035.pdf) found at least 91.3
million acres of public lands managed by the Interior Department — an area
comparable to Montana — could potentially host data centers.

The department’s mandate includes overseeing tribal affairs, managing national
parks, regulating extractive industries like coal and operating dams across
the West. Burgum, though, is spending significant time on other things. This
includes meeting with representatives of companies such as Amazon, Microsoft
and Alphabet more than 20 times from January through November 2025, [according
to a compilation of his schedules](https://www.doi.gov/foia/os/secretarial-
calendars) shared with ProPublica by public interest watchdog group Public
Citizen.

In response, several Democratic senators sent a letter to Burgum in October
saying, “We demand that you immediately cease all efforts to hijack public
lands for the development of data centers, and urge you to provide full
transparency on your role in the DOI’s efforts to site data centers.”

Some of Burgum’s meetings have been previously unreported, including a June
2025 dinner with a high-ranking United Arab Emirates delegation in the wine
room of the upscale Italian restaurant Cafe Milano in Washington’s Georgetown
neighborhood. The small guest list included the United Arab Emirates’ AI lead,
Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, as well as Amos Hochstein, a prominent American
proponent of AI data centers via his investment firm TWG Global.

Several months later, Burgum [signed a memorandum of
understanding](https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/5588362-us-uae-
ai-burgum/) with the Emirati delegation, pledging to work together to deploy
AI.

Neither the Emirati Embassy nor TWG Global responded to requests for comment.

The Interior Department spokesperson said that Burgum “is responsible for
helping unleash American energy production and ensuring our nation has the
resources and infrastructure necessary to lead the future. That mission
requires engagement with industry leaders, stakeholders, and international
partners.”

In an August [Fox News
appearance](https://www.foxnews.com/video/6403873063112) to promote the
administration’s AI efforts, Burgum was asked about the network’s poll showing
70% of voters opposed data centers. He countered by alleging that “foreign
influence” and “misinformation” had played a large role in fueling public
opposition.

Jayson O’Neill, a spokesperson for Save Our Parks, said Burgum and others in
the administration are out of touch with public concerns. “His almost myopic
focus on artificial intelligence and the data center build-out at the expense
of our public lands serves not only the globalist tech titans behind and
within the Trump administration, but also him and the tens of millions of
dollars of his own personal wealth invested in the industry.”

### Potential Conflicts of Interest Across the Administration

Across the administration, political appointees whose offices have AI business
before them hold significant investments in the industry.

[Steve Pearce](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/pearce-stevan/) is director of the Bureau of Land
Management, the Interior Department agency that administers more land than any
other entity in the country. The former New Mexico representative was
confirmed over Democrats’ concerns that he favors selling public lands and
that his career in oil and gas presents a conflict of interest involving an
industry the agency regulates.

But public lands advocates say his AI investments now worry them. Pearce owned
stock in Nvidia, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other AI-
focused companies, according to his most recent publicly available financial
disclosure, signed in October 2025. He also is invested in Titan Development,
a real estate company that has managed several land acquisitions for data
centers in the Southwest. (He pledged to divest many of his AI investments,
but not Titan.)

An agency spokesperson pushed back on the concerns. “Director Pearce complies
with all applicable federal ethics requirements and financial disclosure
obligations,” the spokesperson said in a statement, adding that “conflating
lawful disclosure of financial holdings with an actual conflict of interest
ignores the federal ethics framework designed to identify and address
precisely these questions.”

![A group of people wearing bright green T-shirts with a message written on
the front sit quietly during a Senate confirmation
hearing.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2262985663.jpg?w=2560)Demonstrators wear
shirts stating “Don’t Let Steve Pearce Sell Our Public Lands” during his
Senate confirmation hearing in February to protest the now-Bureau of Land
Management director’s goal of disposing of federally owned land. Bloomberg via
Getty Images

The BLM is reviewing permit applications for about 15 data centers and 17
associated infrastructure projects, including nuclear power plants and
transmission wires, in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Wyoming and Idaho. This
is according to an agency spokesperson and its Mineral & Land Records System.

The project that was to be the first data center on BLM land, near Boulder
City in southern Nevada, had earned a permit to build a solar plant, before
changing its plans. [The BLM approved the
change](https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/judge-orders-pause-on-
boulder-city-data-center) in June without studying the potential environmental
implications. (An Interior Department appeals board has since paused the
project, sending it back to the agency for further review.)

Meanwhile, it remains unclear how much the public will benefit from data
centers on BLM land. The foundational federal land management law was passed
in 1976, so it does not envision data centers. Even so, the department said it
is relying on this statute to permit data centers.

Businesses pay the government to use public land. Oil and gas drillers pay a
royalty on each barrel they produce. Solar power plants pay a per-megawatt
fee.

For data centers, the main charge appears set to be an “annual fair-market-
value rent,” an Interior Department spokesperson said. But such rental fees
can be quite low, so the economic benefit to the public won’t be known until
the data centers are permitted.

![A large scale solar installation on the right and bottom right of the image
borders an open desert landscape.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/AP26285739551521.jpg?w=2560)Federal land overseen by
the Bureau of Land Management was to host a data center near Boulder City,
Nevada, before an Interior Department appeals board paused the project. AP
Photo/John Locher

Another key official with a land management agency who’s heavily invested in
AI is [Michael Boren](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/boren-michael/). He first served as acting assistant
secretary of the Interior Department before transitioning to U.S. Department
of Agriculture undersecretary, where he oversees the Forest Service, second
only to the BLM in the land area it stewards.

Among his many investments in AI companies, Boren reported between about $1.5
million and $6.1 million worth of financial interests in Elon Musk’s xAI,
which has since been acquired by SpaceX. Additionally, he has up to $500,000
invested in Valar Atomics, which is pushing [to build a data center
complex](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5983482/valar-atomic-nuclear-
data-center-project-beehive-utah) called Project Beehive on thousands of acres
of BLM land in Utah, complete with more than 450 small nuclear plants to power
it.

“Undersecretary Boren has fully complied with all federal ethics laws and
requirements and will continue to follow the advice of USDA’s excellent ethics
attorneys,” an Agriculture Department spokesperson said in a statement.

[Lee Zeldin](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-
disclosures/appointees/zeldin-lee/), whom Trump appointed to head the
Environmental Protection Agency, has also emerged as a major AI booster. He
too has dabbled in AI investments. Zeldin’s financial disclosure forms reveal
that in May 2025 he bought and sold up to $15,000 worth of shares of Datavault
AI, a company selling AI-, data- and blockchain-based products.

“Administrator Zeldin followed every ethical rule to a tee in his disclosure
without exception,” an EPA spokesperson said in a statement. The agency added
that he was cleared by its ethics officials and that he has no obligation to
explain such transactions.

The EPA under Zeldin has taken steps to minimize oversight of data centers and
power plants built nearby to keep them running. This includes a rule the
agency proposed in July to end a requirement that states gather public
feedback as they consider air permits for certain facilities, [including data
centers](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/climate/epa-data-centers-public-
comment.html).

In October, a group of Democratic senators [sent a letter to
Zeldin](https://www.kelly.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/kelly-whitehouse-
press-epa-ai-companies-on-rollback-of-public-input-rules-for-data-center-air-
permits/) asking the EPA to withdraw the proposed rule. “The federal
government should encourage transparency and public engagement around these
projects, not make it easier to shroud their construction in secrecy,” they
wrote.

The post [Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Has Tens of
Millions Invested in AI Industry](https://www.propublica.org/article/burgum-
public-land-data-centers-investments) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
